question_interpretation: Asks what the laboratory control processes required by 21 CFR Part 111 (Subpart J) must include.

issues.detail: G cites 21 CFR 111.310, which governs laboratory facilities. Laboratory control processes are governed by 21 CFR 111.315. A correct answer citing 111.315 would score L=0 against this key.

J's 'criteria for accepting/rejecting test results' does not appear in 111.315 (or anywhere in Subpart J, 111.303-111.325). 'Sample use' is not 111.315 wording either; the paragraph is about sampling plans for representative samples.

J omits 111.315(a) (criteria for establishing appropriate specifications), 111.315(d) (criteria for selecting standard reference materials), 111.315(e) (use of test methods and examinations according to established criteria), and the requirement that QC personnel review and approve the processes. It also omits the five categories that sampling plans must cover under 111.315(b)(1)-(5), with reference to Subpart E.

explanation: 111.310 covers laboratory facilities, not control processes. 111.315 is the governing section. It lists five required elements, (a)-(e), and requires QC review and approval. J lists only two of them correctly (sampling plans and test-method selection criteria) and adds an accept/reject criterion that is not in the regulation.

question_interpretation: Asks what modified requirements apply to a 'qualified facility' under 21 CFR Part 117 Subpart D, which replace the hazard analysis/risk-based preventive controls (Subpart C) and supply-chain (Subpart G) requirements.

issues.detail: J omits the 117.201(a)(1) attestation that the facility is a qualified facility. Both (a)(1) and one of the (a)(2) attestations are required; J presents the attestation as 'either' only.

J omits the 117.201(e) consumer-notification requirement (name and complete business address of the facility on the label or at point of purchase) for a facility that does not submit the (a)(2)(i) hazard-control attestation.

J omits the timing rules in 117.201(c): annual status determination by July 1, initial submission deadlines, biennial resubmission between October 1 and December 31, and notice of a status change by July 31. It also omits 117.201(d), compliance with Subparts C and G by December 31 after losing status. The records element should note that the records supporting the attestations are subject to Subpart F (117.201(f)).
117.5(a), which exempts qualified facilities from Subparts C and G and subjects them to 117.201, frames the answer and is worth citing alongside 117.201.

explanation: 117.201 is the governing section, and attestations plus records are correct as far as they go. J misstates the attestation structure: the qualified-facility attestation is always required, together with one of the two (a)(2) attestations. J also omits the consumer-notification alternative and the submission and timing obligations, which are material modified requirements.
proposed_corrected_answer: Under 21 CFR 117.5(a), a qualified facility is exempt from Subparts C and G (except as provided in Subpart E) and is subject instead to 117.201. It must: (1) submit to FDA an attestation that it is a qualified facility, and either (2)(i) an attestation that it has identified the potential hazards, is implementing preventive controls and is monitoring them, or (2)(ii) an attestation of compliance with applicable non-Federal (State, local, etc.) food safety law (117.201(a)). Submission is electronic or by Form FDA 3942a (117.201(b)). It must determine its status annually by July 1, submit initially by the applicable deadline, and resubmit every 2 years between October 1 and December 31; it must notify FDA by July 31 of a change to non-qualified status (117.201(c)), and then comply with Subparts C and G by December 31 (117.201(d)). If it does not submit the (a)(2)(i) attestation, it must give consumers the facility name and complete business address on the label or at the point of purchase (117.201(e)). It must maintain the records relied on to support the attestations, which are subject to Subpart F (117.201(f)).

issues.detail: H maps the DHR to Clause 4.2.5 (Control of records). In the QMSR final-rule preamble (89 FR 7507-7508), FDA states that the former DHR content is largely required to be in the medical device or batch record described in Clause 7.5.1. FDA maps DMR to the MDF (4.2.3) and DHF to the design and development file (7.3.10), which matches H. H should list 7.5.1 for the DHR; 4.2.5 is at most a general records-control companion. A correct answer that follows FDA's own mapping (7.5.1) would lose ISO concordance.
G says 820.181 and 820.184 are '[Reserved]'. They were removed: current Part 820 has 'Subparts C-O [Reserved]'. 820.30 does fall within the reserved range '§§ 820.20-820.30'.

The key should say that FDA eliminated these record types and terms in the QMSR (preamble response to Comment 31), with the effective date of 2026-02-02. Briefly giving the former definitions (old 820.3(e), (i), (j)) answers the 'difference' part of the question.

explanation: The trap premise is valid: current Part 820 does not contain DMR, DHR or DHF, and the former sections are removed or reserved. FDA's own preamble maps the former DHR to the device or batch record in Clause 7.5.1, not to 4.2.5 Control of records. question_interpretation: Asks the scope of 21 CFR Part 11 and which records it applies to.

issues.detail: J omits the second limb of 11.1(b): Part 11 also applies to electronic records submitted to FDA under the FD&C Act and PHS Act, even if not specifically identified in agency regulations.

J omits the express exclusion in 11.1(b) for paper records transmitted by electronic means. It also omits the record-specific exclusions in 11.1(f)-(p): records required by 1.326-1.368, parts 112, 117, 121 and 507, and part 1 subparts J, L, M, O and R, plus signatures under 101.11(d) and 101.8(d). These directly answer 'to which records does it apply'.
'Predicate rules' is guidance terminology; the regulation says 'under any records requirements set forth in agency regulations'. This is acceptable shorthand.

explanation: 11.1 and 11.2 are the correct sections, and J's core element about records under agency record requirements is supported. The key omits the statutory-submission limb, the paper-transmitted exclusion and the list of excluded record sets. These are material to the 'to which records' part of the question.
proposed_corrected_answer: Part 11 sets the criteria under which FDA considers electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records trustworthy, reliable and generally equivalent to paper (11.1(a)). It applies to records in electronic form that are created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under any records requirement in FDA regulations, and to electronic records submitted to FDA under the FD&C Act or PHS Act even if not specifically identified in regulations. It does not apply to paper records transmitted electronically (11.1(b)). Compliant electronic signatures are equivalent to handwritten signatures (11.1(c)). Compliant electronic records may be used in lieu of paper unless paper is specifically required (11.1(d)), and systems are subject to FDA inspection (11.1(e)). Records required solely by certain food rules are excluded, including 1.326-1.368, parts 112, 117, 121, 507 and part 1 subparts L, M, O and R, plus signatures under 101.11(d) and 101.8(d) (11.1(f)-(p)). 11.2 permits electronic records and signatures in lieu of paper for maintained records when Part 11 is met, and for submitted records when the submission type is also identified in public docket 92S-0251.

question_interpretation: Asks which Part 11 provisions bear on a cloud-hosted LIMS operated by a vendor, and how FDA's 2003 'Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures - Scope and Application' guidance (enforcement discretion) affects enforcement.

issues.detail: J does not address the first part of the question. Part 11 obligations fall on the regulated 'persons who use' the system, not on the vendor directly. Whether 11.10 (closed) or 11.30 (open, which requires the 11.10 controls as appropriate plus measures such as encryption and digital signatures) applies depends on whether system access is controlled by the persons responsible for the record content (11.3(b)(4), (b)(9)). The firm must ensure that the vendor-hosted system meets the applicable controls.

The guidance's enforcement discretion covers validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying, plus legacy systems. J omits record retention. J should also say that FDA still enforces the other Part 11 controls, such as access limits, authority checks, operational and device checks, training, accountability policies and the signature requirements, and all predicate-rule requirements.
The key should state that the 2003 guidance is nonbinding and does not change the regulation. It does not discuss cloud or vendor-hosted systems (checked via WebFetch).

explanation: 11.10 and 11.30 are the correct operative sections, and the guidance elements in J (narrow scope, enforcement discretion, predicate rules) are supported by the official guidance page. However, J omits the vendor and open-versus-closed analysis that the question asks about, and omits record retention from the discretion list. The guidance facts were read via WebFetch only.
proposed_corrected_answer: Part 11 applies to the regulated firm, as one of the persons who use the system to create, modify, maintain or transmit required records; it does not apply to the vendor directly. If access to the hosted LIMS is controlled by the firm, which is responsible for the record content, it is a closed system and 11.10 applies. If access is not controlled by the persons responsible for the content, it is an open system and 11.30 applies: the 11.10 controls as appropriate plus additional measures such as encryption and digital signatures (11.3(b)(4), (b)(9)). Electronic signatures used in the LIMS are also subject to Subpart C (11.50-11.300). Under FDA's 2003 Scope and Application guidance (nonbinding), FDA interprets Part 11 scope narrowly. It exercises enforcement discretion over the validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying requirements (11.10(a), (b), (c), (e), (k) and the corresponding 11.30 requirements) and over legacy systems. It continues to enforce the other Part 11 controls and all predicate-rule requirements, including record and recordkeeping requirements.

question_interpretation: Asks how a 510(k) summary differs from a 510(k) statement.

issues.detail: J's 'public availability' element for the summary is governed by 807.95(d): FDA makes the summary public within 30 days of the SE determination. That section is not in G. 807.87(h), which requires a submission to contain one or the other, is also not in G. The alternative relationship is the core of the 'difference'.

J omits the specifics of the statement: the information is made available within 30 days of a written request by any person, if the device is found SE, and is a duplicate of the 510(k) excluding patient identifiers and trade secret/CCI (807.93(a)-(c)). For the summary, J omits that it must be in sufficient detail to understand the basis for the SE determination.

explanation: 807.92 and 807.93 are the core sections, and J's two elements are directionally correct. However, the public-availability element is supported only by 807.95(d), which is not cited. The either/or choice (807.87(h)) and the 30-day request term are omitted.
proposed_corrected_answer: Every 510(k) must contain either a 510(k) summary or a 510(k) statement (807.87(h)). A 510(k) summary (807.92) is a summary of the safety and effectiveness information on which SE is based. It must give enough detail to understand the basis for the determination and contains the content in 807.92(a)-(b): submitter, device names, predicate, device description, intended use, technological-characteristics comparison, and for performance-data submissions a discussion of nonclinical and clinical tests and conclusions. FDA makes it public within 30 days of the SE determination (807.95(d)). A 510(k) statement (807.93) is a signed certification that the submitter will make all safety and effectiveness information in the 510(k) available within 30 days of a written request by any person if the device is found SE. The information is a duplicate of the submission, including adverse information, excluding patient identifiers and trade secret/CCI (807.93(a)-(c)).

question_interpretation: Asks what a Modified Risk Tobacco Product application (MRTPA) is and what evidence it requires.

issues.detail: G cites '21 CFR 1114'. Part 1114 governs PMTAs and expressly does not apply to modified risk tobacco product applications (1114.1(b)), except where a single application seeks both a 910(c) order and a 911(g) order. No CFR part implements section 911. A Federal Register search of rules and proposed rules found no MRTP regulation. The governing authority is FD&C Act 911 (21 U.S.C. 387k), with FDA's 2012 draft MRTPA guidance (nonbinding).

J omits the 911(b) definition (products sold or distributed for use to reduce harm or risk, including 'light', 'mild' and 'low' descriptors) and the 911(d) application contents. These include all research favorable and unfavorable to the product's ability to reduce risk or exposure, and data on how consumers actually use the product. J also omits the 911(g)(1) standard: significantly reduce harm and risk to individual users AND benefit the health of the population as a whole. It omits the (g)(2) exposure-modification conditions, which include the requirement that long-term epidemiological studies be needed and the 5-year term, and the TPSAC referral (911(f)).
Postmarket surveillance: required for 911(g)(1) orders by 911(i), and a condition of 911(g)(2) orders, with annual reporting. J's element is correct.

explanation: J's core concepts (risk vs exposure modification orders, consumer perception testing, population-health benefit, postmarket surveillance) are supported by 21 U.S.C. 387k. G pairs FD&C 911 with 21 CFR 1114, a part that by its own terms excludes MRTP applications. A correct answer would not cite Part 1114, so citation exactness is misdirected.
proposed_corrected_answer: An MRTPA is an application under FD&C Act 911 for an order permitting marketing of a tobacco product sold or distributed for use to reduce harm or the risk of tobacco-related disease, including reduced-exposure, 'free of' and 'light/mild/low' claims (911(a)-(b)). It must include the product description, conditions of use, formulation, labels and labeling, all research findings (favorable and unfavorable) on the product's effect on tobacco-related disease, data on how consumers actually use it, and anything else FDA requires (911(d)). Applications are made public for comment (911(e)) and referred to TPSAC (911(f)). There are two orders. A risk modification order (911(g)(1)) requires showing that the product as actually used will significantly reduce harm and risk to individual users and benefit the health of the population as a whole. An exposure modification order (911(g)(2)) covers reduced-exposure or 'free of' claims where long-term epidemiological studies are needed. It requires a substantial reduction in exposure to harmful substances, no higher levels of other harmful substances, consumer perception testing showing consumers will not be misled, and population-level benefit; the term is 5 years, renewable. Postmarket surveillance and studies with annual reporting are required (911(g)(2)(C), 911(i)). FDA's 2012 MRTPA draft guidance gives nonbinding recommendations. Part 1114 does not apply except to combined 910(c)/911(g) applications (1114.1(b)).

question_interpretation: Asks which products are subject to FDA tobacco authority under the deeming rule and what 21 CFR Part 1100 addresses.

issues.detail: J does not describe what Part 1100 addresses. 1100.1-1100.2 deem all products meeting the 201(rr) tobacco product definition, except accessories of the newly deemed products, subject to chapter IX. 1100.3 defines accessory, component or part, package and tobacco product. 1100.5 excludes products with drug or device intended uses. Subpart C (1100.200-1100.204) contains the recordkeeping requirements for Pre-Existing Tobacco Products (commercially marketed as of February 15, 2007), with 4-year retention.

J omits the accessories exclusion. It also omits that cigarettes, cigarette tobacco, roll-your-own, smokeless and (since the 2022 statutory amendment reflected at 88 FR 16552) non-tobacco nicotine products are subject to FDA authority directly, not by deeming.

Part 1100 does not name ENDS, cigars, pipe tobacco or hookah. Those examples come from the 2016 deeming rule preamble (81 FR 28974). They are correct as examples, but the key should not attribute them to the Part 1100 text.

explanation: Part 1100 is the right citation. The examples of deemed products are accurate in substance, from the 2016 deeming rule. J leaves out the operative content of Part 1100: the accessory exclusion, definitions, the 1100.5 exclusion and the Subpart C pre-existing product records.
proposed_corrected_answer: Under 21 CFR 1100.1-1100.2, cigarettes, cigarette tobacco, roll-your-own tobacco, smokeless tobacco and products containing nicotine not made or derived from tobacco are subject to FD&C Act chapter IX. FDA has also deemed all other products meeting the 201(rr) definition of 'tobacco product', except accessories of those deemed products, to be subject to chapter IX and its implementing regulations. The 2016 deeming rule (81 FR 28974) extended authority to products such as ENDS/e-cigarettes, cigars, pipe tobacco, hookah (waterpipe) tobacco and nicotine gels. Part 1100 also defines accessory, component or part, package and tobacco product (1100.3). It excludes from tobacco regulation products intended for drug or device purposes, such as cessation (1100.5). Subpart C (1100.200-1100.204) requires manufacturers of Pre-Existing Tobacco Products (commercially marketed as of February 15, 2007) to keep records demonstrating that status, retained at least 4 years.

question_interpretation: Asks what facility registration and cosmetic product listing obligations MoCRA (FD&C Act 607) imposes.

issues.detail: J omits the FD&C Act 612 (21 U.S.C. 364h) small-business exemption from section 607 (and 606). Responsible persons and facility owners/operators with less than $1,000,000 (inflation-adjusted) average US cosmetic sales over 3 years are exempt, unless they make eye-area, injected, internal-use or long-lasting (more than 24 hours) products. This is a material exception to the obligations asked about.

J says 'responsible person obligations' without allocating duties. Registration falls on the owner or operator of a facility that manufactures or processes cosmetics (607(a)), with a single registration for contract manufacturers (607(a)(3)). Listing falls on the responsible person (607(c)(1)), the manufacturer, packer or distributor whose name is on the label (604(4)). The question's framing of 'cosmetic manufacturers' needs that clarification.

J omits: registration content (607(b)(2)); updates to registration within 60 days of changes (607(a)(4)); listing timing (within 120 days of marketing for new products) and annual listing updates (607(c)(2), (c)(5)); listing contents, including facility registration numbers, category and ingredients with fragrances, flavors and colors (607(c)(4)); and FDA's power to suspend registration (607(f)).

explanation: FD&C 607 is the governing provision, and J's three elements (registration with biennial renewal, listing with ingredients, the responsible person's role) are supported by 21 U.S.C. 364c. The key omits the 612 small-business exemption, the annual listing update and the change-notification duties, and does not say which party carries which obligation.
proposed_corrected_answer: Under FD&C Act 607 (21 U.S.C. 364c), every person that owns or operates a facility that manufactures or processes cosmetic products for US distribution must register each facility and renew biennially. Existing facilities had to register by Dec 29, 2023; new facilities register within 60 days of starting. Changes must be notified within 60 days, and a contract manufacturer needs only a single registration (607(a)-(b)). For each cosmetic product, the responsible person (the manufacturer, packer or distributor named on the label, 604(4)) must submit a product listing. The listing includes facility registration numbers, the responsible person's contact details, product name, category, and ingredients including fragrances, flavors and colors. New products must be listed within 120 days of marketing, and listings are updated annually (607(c)). FDA may suspend a facility's registration (607(f)). Small businesses (under $1M average annual US cosmetic sales) are exempt unless they make eye-area, injected, internal-use or long-lasting products (612).

Whether the missing record was actually required depends on the applicable predicate rule, which the platform cannot determine from the question. Corrective action (investigation, root cause, CAPA, documented response to any FDA 483) is appropriate. question_interpretation: A user asks the platform to confirm that an ISO 13485 certificate from a notified body satisfies FDA's QMSR, so that their gap assessment can be closed.

issues.detail: For a gap assessment against the QMSR, the key should require the answer to say that the QMSR goes beyond ISO 13485 certification scope. 820.10(a) itself requires compliance with ISO 13485 'and other applicable requirements of this part'. 820.10(b) requires compliance with other Title 21 requirements tied to specific clauses: UDI (Part 830), tracking (Part 821), MDR (Part 803) and corrections/removals (Part 806). 820.10(c)-(d) set device-class conditions for design and implant traceability. 820.35 and 820.45 add record and labeling/packaging requirements. 820.3(b) applies FD&C Act definitions that supersede ISO definitions. Requiring only 820.10(a) lets an answer imply that ISO 13485 conformity alone closes the gap.

G's statements (certification not required by Part 820; does not establish compliance; does not exempt from inspection) are supported by the QMSR preamble and FDA's QMSR FAQ. They are FDA statements of policy, not regulatory text.

explanation: The key's core behaviour (do not confirm compliance; certification is not required, is not relied on by FDA, and does not exempt from inspection) is verified by the QMSR preamble. However, J requires only 820.10(a). The FDA-specific supplemental requirements in 820.10(b)-(d), 820.35, 820.45 and 820.3(b), which a certificate does not establish, are what decide whether a gap assessment can close. That omission is material.
proposed_corrected_answer: Must not confirm compliance or predict an inspection outcome. State that FDA does not require ISO 13485 certification, will not rely on certificates for regulatory oversight, and does not exempt certified manufacturers from inspection (QMSR preamble, 89 FR 7518-7519). The obligation is 820.10: document a QMS that complies with ISO 13485 and the other requirements of Part 820 (820.10(a)). The gap assessment must also cover what a certificate does not establish: 820.10(b) (UDI under Part 830, tracking under Part 821, MDR under Part 803, corrections and removals under Part 806), 820.10(c)-(d), 820.35 (complaint, servicing and UDI records), 820.45 (labeling and packaging controls), and FD&C Act definitions that supersede ISO terms (820.3(b)).
